categories.name: Boycott / conflict complicity
categories.description: Named in active boycott campaigns, or material involvement in an ongoing armed conflict or occupation.

categories.name: Human rights
categories.description: Documented human rights abuses not already covered by labor rights (e.g. surveillance of dissidents, complicity in state repression).

categories.name: Labor rights
categories.description: Forced labor, unsafe working conditions, union-busting, wage theft, exploitative supply-chain practices.

categories.name: Environment
categories.description: Significant pollution, deforestation, greenwashing found to be materially false, or major climate-related harm.

categories.name: Animal welfare
categories.description: Animal testing beyond legal requirement, factory-farming practices, documented cruelty in supply chain.

categories.name: Corruption
categories.description: Bribery, embezzlement, or other corrupt practices confirmed by investigation, conviction, or credible reporting.

categories.name: Tax avoidance
categories.description: Aggressive tax avoidance structures (e.g. profit shifting) beyond routine legal optimization.

categories.name: Political influence
categories.description: Lobbying or political donations directed at undermining regulation, human rights, or democratic process.

categories.name: Data privacy
categories.description: Confirmed misuse of user data, surveillance overreach, or major data-protection violations.

categories.name: Anti-competitive practices
categories.description: Confirmed antitrust violations, predatory pricing, or market-dominance abuse.

categories.name: Financial misconduct
categories.description: Fraud, mis-selling, improper fee/premium practices, or risk-control failures that harmed customers or investors — distinct from corruption (which implies bribery or self-dealing).

flags.description: Allianz Global Investors U.S. pleaded guilty to criminal securities fraud in 2022 after three of its senior portfolio managers orchestrated a multi-year scheme to conceal the true risk of its 'Structured Alpha' funds from roughly 114 institutional investors (including pension funds), who invested around $11 billion. The fraud caused over $5 billion in investor losses; Allianz paid over $1 billion in SEC penalties plus more than $5 billion total in restitution, and AGI US was barred from advising US-registered mutual funds and certain pension funds.

Nivea (Beiersdorf) pulled a 2017 deodorant ad captioned 'White is Purity' after backlash that it echoed white-supremacist rhetoric equating whiteness with purity; it was the second such incident in six years after a 2011 ad telling a Black man to 're-civilize' himself.

Although Carlsberg stopped production of its own Carlsberg- and Tuborg-branded beer in Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, other Carlsberg-owned brands continued to be sold there via its Baltika subsidiary; in July 2023 the Russian government seized Carlsberg's stake in Baltika under a decree targeting companies from 'unfriendly' countries, and Carlsberg only completed an exit sale in December 2024.

Chocolat Frey ranked 26th (last among assessed Swiss producers) in the 2025 Chocolate Scorecard, an annual NGO/university-run assessment, which cited Migros as having the most room for improvement on cocoa-supply-chain transparency and pesticide use; Migros acknowledged the gap and pointed to a newer sustainability strategy including traceable certified cocoa and an anti-child-labor project in Ghana.

A Coca-Cola bottling plant in Plachimada, Kerala (India) had its operating licence revoked in 2003 amid findings of water scarcity and environmental damage; a 2010 government-appointed committee recommended the company pay about $48 million in damages, and the plant was permanently abandoned in 2017 after years of litigation.

In 2015, Coca-Cola provided $1 million to launch the Global Energy Balance Network, a research group that promoted the message that physical inactivity, not sugary drinks, was the primary driver of obesity; the network disbanded within a year after reporting exposed Coca-Cola's role in shaping its message and choosing its leadership.
Switzerland's highest court ruled that a CHF 80 million capital transfer Concordia had used to prop up its mandatory basic-insurance business was unlawful, following a multi-year legal dispute.

Coop and Migros together account for roughly 80% of Swiss grocery retail sales; Swiss consumer-protection group Konsumentenschutz has publicly called on the competition commission (WEKO) to act against the pair over high margins and large price gaps on organic food.

Credit Suisse agreed in 2021 to pay roughly $475–547 million combined to US and UK authorities (including a $100 million SEC settlement) over fraud and FCPA violations in Mozambique's 'tuna bonds' scandal, where bankers received $50 million in hidden kickbacks for arranging loans nominally meant for a state tuna-fishing fleet and coast guard.

Following the March 2021 collapse of Archegos Capital, which cost Credit Suisse $5.5 billion, an independent review found the losses resulted from a fundamental failure of management and controls; the UK's PRA fined the bank £87 million in 2023 and Swiss regulator FINMA found Credit Suisse had 'seriously and systematically' breached financial market laws.

Switzerland's financial regulator FINMA ordered CSS to reimburse CHF 129 million to supplementary-insurance policyholders after finding it had improperly folded unjustified administrative costs into premium calculations from 2013 to 2019. CSS is contesting the ruling before the Federal Administrative Court, so it is not yet legally final.

Danone was among several companies that suspended palm oil sourcing from First Resources after a 2021 investigation found the supplier controlled a network of shadow companies responsible for more deforestation in Southeast Asia than any other palm oil company.

A local trout farmer sued Danone's Volvic operation after the stream feeding his fish farm dried up, separately also suing the French state; annual water pumping for the Volvic brand grew from about 200,000 litres in 1950 to 1.7 billion litres in 2020, raising local concern about groundwater depletion.

fenaco, the cooperative federation controlling roughly 80% of Swiss farmers' upstream/downstream supply chain, has been repeatedly criticized (including by NZZ and think-tank Avenir Suisse) for using its dominant market position to pay producers — for example wine and cider growers — prices below production cost while extracting high margins at the retail end due to limited competition.
Galenica announced in 2025 a consultation on cutting up to 170 jobs at its Bichsel subsidiary, stating prior measures to improve results had not been sufficient.

In 2022 Glencore pleaded guilty in the US to conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, admitting to paying over $100 million in bribes to officials in Nigeria, Cameroon, Ivory Coast, Equatorial Guinea, DR Congo, Venezuela and Brazil between 2007 and 2018, as part of a combined global resolution exceeding $1.1 billion.
In the same 2022 resolution, Glencore's US subsidiary separately pleaded guilty to a conspiracy to manipulate fuel oil price benchmarks at US ports via a South Africa-based trading desk.

The Changing Markets Foundation found that roughly 60-96% of sustainability claims tied to H&M's "Conscious Collection" were unsubstantiated or misleading; a related 2022 US class-action lawsuit alleged the collection often contained more synthetic fiber than H&M's regular lines despite being marketed as more sustainable.

Investigative NGO Earthsight documented an IKEA supplier's involvement in illegally logging roughly 4 million trees over a decade in protected, climate-critical forests in Siberia, despite FSC audits failing to flag it.

IKEA acknowledged that political prisoners in communist East Germany were used as forced labor to produce components for its furniture in the 1970s-80s, and pledged €6 million in 2024 to a fund compensating survivors.

In 2011, Brazilian labor inspectors found migrant workers in slavery-like conditions (16-hour days, restricted movement) at a São Paulo workshop producing garments for Zara via a subcontracted supplier. Zara Brasil lost the resulting court case and its appeal, with the case closing in November 2017.

French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened an investigation in July 2021 into Inditex and three other multinationals over alleged profiting from Uyghur forced labor in Xinjiang supply chains; Canada's ombudsperson (CORE) opened a separate probe into Zara in November 2023 following a civil-society complaint.

Julius Bär booked CHF 606 million in write-downs in 2023 and a further CHF 586 million in credit losses in early 2024 tied to loans to René Benko's collapsed Signa real-estate group; FINMA opened enforcement proceedings over insufficient separation between the bank's risk-control and business functions, and the bank's CEO left as a result.

A 2024 BBC World Service investigation found children as young as five picking jasmine overnight for as little as $1/day on Egyptian farms supplying fragrance suppliers used by L'Oréal; L'Oréal acknowledged certain supplier practices don't meet its commitments.

Animal-rights groups do not recognize L'Oréal as cruelty-free because it continues to sell finished cosmetics in mainland China, where regulators have required animal testing for certain product categories.

Mars is named, alongside Cargill, Mondelez, Nestlé, Hershey, Olam, and Barry Callebaut, in ongoing US lawsuits (including a 2021 case brought by eight former child laborers, with litigation continuing as of 2023) alleging the companies knowingly sourced cocoa harvested by child and forced laborers on Ivory Coast plantations.

Migros announced a restructuring in May 2024 cutting an initial 150 head-office jobs as part of a wider plan to eliminate around 1,500 positions and close specialist store formats (e.g. Melectronics, Do it + Garden), stated as aimed at 'simplified processes, lean structures and clear roles.'

Migros is listed as a contacted stakeholder (Uyghur-labor concern category) in The Outlaw Ocean Project's investigation into forced labor in Chinese seafood processing; the investigation traced MSC-certified cod from supplier Donggang Jinhui, and seafood from Donggang Haimeng via Riberalves, into products sold on Migros's shelves and website.

Migros and Coop together account for roughly 80% of Swiss grocery retail sales; Swiss consumer-protection group Konsumentenschutz has publicly called on the competition commission (WEKO) to act against the pair over high margins and large price gaps on organic food.

Mondelez continued operating three factories in Russia after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, reporting $1.417 billion in Russian revenue and paying over $62 million in profit taxes to the Russian government in 2024; Ukraine's anti-corruption agency designated it an 'International Sponsor of War' in 2023, and Buckingham Palace revoked its Cadbury brand's royal warrant in December 2024 over the continued operations.

Nestlé has been the target of an international consumer boycott, ongoing since 1989, over marketing of infant formula in developing countries in ways that critics and independent audits say violate the WHO's International Code of Marketing of Breast-Milk Substitutes.

Through the 1990s, Nike's contract factories in Indonesia and Vietnam were documented (starting with a 1991 report by Jeff Ballinger) subjecting workers to poverty wages, excessive overtime, and unsafe conditions; CEO Phil Knight publicly acknowledged unfair labor practices in a May 1998 speech and committed to reforms, leading to the 1999 founding of the Fair Labor Association.

In 2020 Novartis AG and its former subsidiary Alcon agreed to pay a combined $345 million to the US DOJ and SEC to resolve Foreign Corrupt Practices Act charges, admitting employees bribed government-employed healthcare providers in Greece, Vietnam and South Korea to boost sales (following a separate, smaller 2016 FCPA settlement over conduct in China).

Oatly's 2020 acceptance of a $200 million investment from Blackstone (alongside celebrity co-investors) triggered a consumer boycott after Blackstone was reported to be a part-owner of two Brazilian firms linked to Amazon deforestation; the deforestation link is to Oatly's investor, not to Oatly's own operations, which Oatly has publicly defended.

Break Free From Plastic's annual global brand audits have repeatedly named PepsiCo among the world's top plastic polluters for several consecutive years, based on volunteer-collected plastic waste counts across dozens of countries.

A 2016 report by Rainforest Action Network, OPPUK, and the International Labor Rights Forum documented child labor, hazardous pesticide exposure, and below-minimum-wage pay on Indonesian palm oil plantations supplying PepsiCo through its partner Indofood; PepsiCo suspended sourcing from Indofood in 2018 pending progress on the issues.

Rainforest Action Network documented illegal palm oil plantations inside the protected Leuser Ecosystem in Sumatra linked to P&G's supply chain, and reports P&G has repeatedly failed to fulfill its public commitments to restore the destroyed rainforest.
Rainforest Action Network reports P&G has knowingly sourced palm oil tied to forced-labor practices for brands including Head & Shoulders, Pantene, and Gillette.

Former Raiffeisen CEO Pierin Vincenz (1999-2015) was convicted in 2022 by the Zurich District Court and sentenced to 3 years and 9 months in prison for fraud, breach of trust, and document forgery, after secretly holding stakes in companies he then had Raiffeisen and its Aduno subsidiary acquire without disclosing his conflict of interest. The Swiss Federal Supreme Court upheld the conviction; an appeal on sentencing continues.

Pakistani workers at a Florence subcontractor producing Montblanc leather goods were paid roughly €3/hour for up to 70-hour weeks; after unionizing and winning legal working conditions, Richemont dropped the supplier, and in January 2025 filed a defamation/coercion complaint against the union organizers, which labor-rights groups characterize as a SLAPP suit.

South Africa's Competition Commission is prosecuting Roche over allegedly excessive pricing of the breast cancer drug trastuzumab (Herceptin), estimating that around 10,000 women were unable to afford the roughly $32,000/year treatment between 2011 and 2019 as a result; the Commission has described the pricing as a violation of basic human rights and is seeking maximum penalties. This is an ongoing case, not yet concluded.
A BBC investigation found workers at Shein's Chinese supplier factories working up to 75-hour weeks, exceeding Chinese labor-law limits, for pay below living-wage standards.

The US House Select Committee on the CCP released interim findings in September 2024 from a bipartisan investigation into Shein's and Temu's potential supply-chain ties to Uyghur forced labor and Xinjiang cotton; Shein says tests show about 2.1% of its cotton originates from the region and that it has since stopped sourcing cotton from China, a claim disputed by lawmakers.

UBS agreed in 2023 to pay France roughly €835 million to settle a long-running case over illegally soliciting wealthy clients in France to hide money in undeclared Swiss accounts between 2004 and 2012; a French court had originally fined UBS a record €4.5 billion in 2019 for tax fraud and money laundering, later reduced on appeal.

A 2016 Amnesty International investigation traced palm oil from Wilmar plantations in Indonesia — where children as young as 8 worked in hazardous conditions without protective equipment — into Unilever's supply chain; Unilever confirmed it bought palm oil from Wilmar.

Unilever continued operating in Russia for over two years after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, only completing the sale of its Russian business in October 2024; Ukraine's anti-corruption agency designated it an 'International Sponsor of War' in July 2023 citing its tax contributions to the Russian state, and Buckingham Palace revoked its royal warrant in December 2024 over the continued operations.

In September 2025, historian Anne Sudrow's research (published under the Dachau Memorial's auspices, first reported by Der Spiegel) revealed Weleda skin cream was used by SS doctor Sigmund Rascher in brutal Nazi freezing experiments on roughly 300 Dachau prisoners to test frostbite prevention, of whom an estimated 80-90 died; Weleda announced it would re-investigate its Nazi-era history after previously concluding no direct link existed.
